entries.2caca82d15ea315986998240856515bb0408cfd4: <div sID="gen19940" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Hos.13" sID="Hos.13"/> <div eID="gen19940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19941" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19942" type="x-p"/> The same strings, though generally unpleasing ones, are harped upon in this chapter that were in those before. People care not to be told either of their sin or of their danger by sin; and yet it is necessary, and for their good, that they should be told of both, nor can they better hear of either than from the word of God and from their faithful ministers, while the sin may be repented of and the danger prevented. Here, I. The people of Israel are reproved and threatened for their idolatry, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.1-Hos.13.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. They are reproved and threatened for their wantonness, pride, and luxury, and other abuses of their wealth and prosperity, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.5-Hos.13.8">ver. 5-8</reference>. III. The ruin that is coming upon them for these and all their other sins is foretold as very terrible, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.12-Hos.13.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.15">15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.16">16</reference>. IV. Those among them that yet retain a respect for their God are here encouraged to hope that he will yet appear for their relief, though their kings and princes, and all their other supports and succours, fail them, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.9-Hos.13.11">ver. 9-11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.14">14</reference>.
entries.32b31357eaf05093aa97352f6600a9b11f5f67d3: <div eID="gen19942" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19941" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Reproofs and Threatenings. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 722.)</title> <div sID="gen19943" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When Ephraim spake trembling, he exalted himself in Israel; but when he offended in Baal, he died. <hi type="super">2</hi> And now they sin more and more, and have made them molten images of their silver, <hi type="italic">and</hi> idols according to their own understanding, all of it the work of the craftsmen: they say of them, Let the men that sacrifice kiss the calves. <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud, and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff <hi type="italic">that</hi> is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney. <hi type="super">4</hi> Yet I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God from the land of Egypt, and thou shalt know no god but me: for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no saviour beside me. <div eID="gen19943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19944" type="x-p"/> Idolatry was the sin that did most easily beset the Jewish nation till after the captivity; the ten tribes from the first were guilty of it, but especially after the days of Ahab; and this is the sin which, in these verses, they are charged with. Observe, <div eID="gen19944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19945" type="x-p"/> I. The provision that God made to prevent their falling into idolatry. This we have, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.4">v. 4</reference>. God did what was fit to be done to keep them close to himself; what could have been done more? 1. He made known himself to them as <hi type="italic">the Lord their God,</hi> and took them to be his people in a peculiar manner. Both by his word and by his works all along <hi type="italic">from the land of Egypt</hi> he declared, <hi type="italic">I am the Lord thy God;</hi> he told them so from heaven at Mount Sinai, that he was <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">their God,</hi> who <hi type="italic">brought them out of the land of Egypt.</hi> This he continued both to declare and to prove to them by his prophets and by his providences. 2. He gave them a law forbidding them to worship any other: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt know no God but me;</hi> not only shalt not own and worship any other, but shalt not acquaint thyself with any other, nor make the rites and usages of the Gentiles familiar to thee." Note, It is a happy ignorance not to know that which we ought not to meddle with. We find those commended who <hi type="italic">have not known the depths of Satan.</hi> 3. He gave them a good reason for it: <hi type="italic">There is no saviour besides me.</hi> Whatever we take for our God we expect to have for our saviour, to make us happy here and hereafter; as, where we have protection, we owe allegiance, so where we have salvation, and hope for it, we owe adoration. <div eID="gen19945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19946" type="x-p"/> II. The honour that Ephraim had, while he kept himself clear from idolatry (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">While Ephraim spoke trembling,</hi> or <hi type="italic">with trembling</hi> (that is, as Dr. Pocock understands it, while he behaved himself towards God as his father Jacob did, with <hi type="italic">weeping and supplications,</hi> and spoke not proudly and insolently against God and his prophets, while he kept up a holy fear of God, and worshipped him in that fear) so long <hi type="italic">he exalted himself in Israel,</hi> that is, he was very considerable among the tribes and made a figure. Jeroboam, who was of that tribe, exalted himself and his family. <hi type="italic">When he spoke there was trembling,</hi> that is, all about him stood in awe of him; so some understand it. Note, <hi type="italic">Those that humble themselves,</hi> especially that humble themselves before God, <hi type="italic">shall be exalted.</hi> When people speak with modesty and jealousy of themselves, with a diffidence of their own judgment and a deference to others, they exalt themselves, they gain a reputation. But as for Ephraim he soon lost himself: <hi type="italic">When he offended in Baal he died,</hi> that is, he lost his reputation, his honour soon dwindled and sunk, and was laid in the dust. Baal is here put for all idolatry; when Ephraim forsook God, and took to worship images, the state received its death's wound and was never good for any thing afterwards. Note, Deserting God is the death of any person or persons. <div eID="gen19946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19947" type="x-p"/> III. The lamentable growth of idolatry among them (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now they sin more and more.</hi> When once he began to <hi type="italic">offend in Baal</hi> the ice was broken, and he grew worse and worse, coveted more idols, doted more upon those he had, and grew more ridiculous in the worship of them. Note, The way of idolatry, as of other sins, is down-hill, and men cannot easily stop themselves. It is the sad case of all those who have forsaken God that they sin yet more and more. Let us trace them in their apostasy. 1. They made themselves <hi type="italic">molten images,</hi> proud to have gods that they could cast into what mould they pleased; probably these were the calves in miniature like the silver shrines for Diana; the zealots for the calf-worship carried about with them, it may be, images of the gods they worshipped, made on purpose <hi type="italic">for themselves.</hi> 2. They made them of <hi type="italic">their silver,</hi> and then doubted not of their property in them, when they purchased them with their own money or made them of their own plate melted down for that purpose. See what cost they put themselves to in the service of their idols, which they honoured with the best they had, and therefore made their molten images of silver. 3. They made them <hi type="italic">according to their own understanding,</hi> according to their own fancy. They consulted with themselves what shape they should make their idol in, and made it accordingly, <hi type="italic">a god</hi> according to the <hi type="italic">best of their judgment.</hi> Or <hi type="italic">according to their own likeness,</hi> in the form of a man. And, when they made their idols men like themselves in shape, they made themselves stocks and stones like them in reality; for <hi type="italic">those that make them are like unto them, and so is every one that trusts in them.</hi> 4. It was <hi type="italic">all the work of the craftsmen.</hi> Their images did not pretend, like that of Diana, to have come down from Jupiter (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.35">Acts xix. 35</reference>); no, perhaps the workmen stamped their names upon them, such an idol was such a man's work. See <reference osisRef="Hos.8.6">ch. viii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Isa. xliv. 9</reference>, &c. 5. Though they were thus the work of their hands, yet they were the beloved of their souls; for they say of them, <hi type="italic">Let the men that sacrifice kiss the calves.</hi> Either the priests called upon the people thus to pay their homage, or the people, who were not allowed to come so near themselves, called upon the <hi type="italic">men that sacrificed,</hi> the priests that attended for them, to <hi type="italic">kiss the calves</hi> in their name and stead, because they could not reach to do it, so very fond were they of paying their utmost respects to such an idol as they were taught to have a veneration for. Though they were calves, yet, if they were gods, the worshippers, by themselves or their proxies, thus made their honours to them. They <hi type="italic">kissed the calves,</hi> in token of the adoration of them, affection for them, and allegiance to them, as theirs. Thus we are directed to <hi type="italic">kiss the Son,</hi> to take him for our Lord and our God. <div eID="gen19947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19948" type="x-p"/> IV. Threatenings of wrath for their idolatry. The Lord, whose name is <hi type="italic">Jealous,</hi> is a jealous God, and will not give his glory to another; and therefore all those that <hi type="italic">worship images</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">confounded,</hi> especially if Ephraim do it, <reference osisRef="Ps.97.7">Ps. xcvii. 7</reference>. Because they are so fond of kissing their calves, therefore God will give them sensible convictions of their folly, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.3">v. 3</reference>. They promise themselves a great deal of safety and satisfaction in the worship of their idols, and that their prosperity will thereby be established; but God tells them that they shall be disappointed, and <hi type="italic">driven away in their wickedness.</hi> This is illustrated by four similitudes:—They shall be, 1. As the <hi type="italic">morning cloud,</hi> which promises showers of rain to the parched ground. 2. As the <hi type="italic">early dew,</hi> which seems to be an earnest of such showers. But both <hi type="italic">pass away,</hi> and the day proves as dry and hot as ever; so fleet and transitory their profession of piety was (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">ch. vi. 4</reference>), and so had they disappointed God's expectation from them, and therefore it is just that so their prosperity should be, and so their expectations from their idols should be disappointed, and so will all theirs be that make an idol of this world. 3. They are <hi type="italic">as the chaff,</hi> light and worthless; and they shall be driven <hi type="italic">as the chaff is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.1.4">Ps. i. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">xxv. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.18">Job xxi. 18</reference>. Nay, 4. They are <hi type="italic">as the smoke,</hi> noisome and offensive (see <reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Isa. lxv. 5</reference>), and they shall be driven away <hi type="italic">as the smoke out of the chimneys,</hi> that is soon dissipated and disappears, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.2">Ps. lxviii. 2</reference>. Note, No solid lasting comfort is to be expected any where but in God.
entries.4eeaf7691105b1189012f618d519b151c66b935a: <div eID="gen19948" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ingratitude of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 722.)</title> <div sID="gen19949" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> I did know thee in the wilderness, in the land of great drought. <hi type="super">6</hi> According to their pasture, so were they filled; they were filled, and their heart was exalted; therefore have they forgotten me. <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore I will be unto them as a lion: as a leopard by the way will I observe <hi type="italic">them:</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> I will meet them as a bear <hi type="italic">that is</hi> bereaved <hi type="italic">of her whelps,</hi> and will rend the caul of their heart, and there will I devour them like a lion: the wild beast shall tear them. <div eID="gen19949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19950" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, 1. The plentiful provision God had made for Israel and the seasonable supplies he had blessed them with (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I did know thee in the wilderness,</hi> took cognizance of thy case and made provision for thee, even in <hi type="italic">a land of great drought,</hi> when thou wast in extreme distress, and when no relief was to be had in an ordinary way." See a description of this wilderness, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">Deut. viii. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jer. ii. 6</reference>, and say, The God that knew them, and owned them, and fed them there, was a <hi type="italic">friend indeed,</hi> for he was a <hi type="italic">friend at need</hi> and an all-sufficient friend, that could victual so vast an army when all ordinary ways of provision were cut off, and where, if miracles had not been their daily bread, they must all have perished. Note, Help at an exigency lays under peculiar obligations and must never be forgotten. 2. Their unworthy ungrateful abuse of God's favour to them. God not only took care of them in the wilderness, but put them in possession of Canaan, a good land, a large and fat pasture. And (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">v. 6</reference>) <hi type="italic">according to their pasture so were they filled.</hi> God gave them both plenty and dainties, and they did not spare it, but, having been long confined to manna, when they came into Canaan they fed themselves <hi type="italic">to the full.</hi> And this was no hopeful presage; it would have looked better, and promised better, if they had been more modest and moderate in the use of their plenty, and had learned to deny themselves; but what was the effect of it? <hi type="italic">They were filled, and their heart was exalted.</hi> Their luxury and sensuality made them proud, insolent, and secure. The best comment upon this is that of Moses, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13-Deut.32.15">Deut. xxxii. 13-15</reference>. But <hi type="italic">Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked.</hi> When the body was stuffed up with plenty the soul was puffed up with pride. Then they began to think their religion a thing below them, and they could not persuade themselves to stoop to the services of it. <hi type="italic">The wicked, through the pride of his countenance, will not seek after God.</hi> When they were poor and lame in the wilderness they thought it was necessary for them to keep in with God; but when they were replenished and established in Canaan they began to think they had no further need of him: <hi type="italic">Their heart was exalted, therefore have they forgotten me.</hi> Note, Worldly prosperity, when it feeds men's pride, makes them forgetful of God; for they remember him only when they want him. When Israel was filled, what more could the Almighty do for them? And therefore they said to him, <hi type="italic">Depart from us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.22.17">Job xxii. 17</reference>. It is sad that those favours which ought to make us mindful of God, and studious what we shall render to him, should make us unmindful of him, and regardless what we do against him. We ought to know that we live upon God when we live upon common providence, though we do not, as Israel in the wilderness, live upon miracles. 3. God's just resentment of their base ingratitude, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.7-Hos.14.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. The judgments threatened (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.3">v. 3</reference>) intimated the departure of all good from them. The threatenings here go further, and intimate the breaking in of all evils upon them; for God, who had so much befriended them, now <hi type="italic">turns to be their enemy and fights against them,</hi> which is expressed here very terribly: <hi type="italic">I will be unto them as a lion</hi> and <hi type="italic">as a leopard.</hi> The lion is strong, and there is no resisting him. The leopard is here taken notice of to be crafty and vigilant: <hi type="italic">As a leopard by the way will I observe them.</hi> As that beast of prey lies in wait by the road-side to catch travellers, and devour them, so will God by his judgments <hi type="italic">watch over them</hi> to do them hurt, as he had watched over them to do them good, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.27">Jer. xliv. 27</reference>. No opportunity shall be let slip that may accelerate or aggravate their ruin (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.6">Jer. v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">A leopard shall watch over their cities.</hi> A lynx, or spotted beast (and such the leopard is), is noted for quicksightedness above any creature (<hi type="italic">lynx visu—the eyes of a lynx</hi>), and so it intimates that not only the power, but the wisdom of God is engaged against those whom he has a controversy with. Some read it (and the original will bear it), <hi type="italic">I will be as a leopard in the way of Assyria.</hi> The judgments of God shall surprise them just when they are going to the Assyrians to seek for protection and help from them. It is added, <hi type="italic">I will meet them as a bear that is bereaved,</hi> and thereby exasperated and made more cruel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.17.8">2 Sam. xvii. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.15">Prov. xxviii. 15</reference>), which intimates how highly God was provoked, and he would make them feel it: He will <hi type="italic">rend the caul of their heart.</hi> The lion is observed to aim at the heart of the beasts he preys upon, and thus will God <hi type="italic">devour them like a lion.</hi> He will send such judgments upon them as shall prey upon their spirits and consume their vitals. Their heart was exalted (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">v. 6</reference>), but God will take an effectual course to bring it down: <hi type="italic">The wild beast shall tear them;</hi> not only God will be as a lion and leopard to them, but the metaphor shall be fulfilled in the letter, for <hi type="italic">noisome beasts</hi> are one of the <hi type="italic">four sore judgments</hi> with which God will destroy a provoking people, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.15">Ezek. xiv. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen19950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19951" type="x-p"/> Now all this teaches us, 1. That abused goodness turns into the greater severity. Those who despise God and affront him, when he is to them as a careful tender shepherd, shall find he will be even to his own flock as the beasts of prey are. Those whom God has in vain <hi type="italic">endured with much long-suffering,</hi> and invited with much affection, in them he will <hi type="italic">show his wrath</hi> and make them <hi type="italic">vessels</hi> of it, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.22">Rom. ix. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Patientia læsa fit furor</hi>—<hi type="italic">Despised patience will turn into fury.</hi> 2. That the judgments of God, when they come with commission against impenitent sinners, will be irresistible and very terrible. They will <hi type="italic">rend the caul of the heart,</hi> will fill the soul with confusion, and tear that in pieces; and we are as unable to grapple with them as a lamb is to make his part good against a roaring lion, for <hi type="italic">who knows the power of God's anger? Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord,</hi> let us be persuaded to make peace with him; for are we stronger then he?
entries.945f360033be49861c70ed8413d8c32aeda03975: <div eID="gen19951" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Folly of Israel; Promises of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 722.)</title> <div sID="gen19952" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> O Israel, thou hast destroyed thyself; but in me <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine help. <hi type="super">10</hi> I will be thy king: where <hi type="italic">is any other</hi> that may save thee in all thy cities? and thy judges of whom thou saidst, Give me a king and princes? <hi type="super">11</hi> I gave thee a king in mine anger, and took <hi type="italic">him</hi> away in my wrath. <hi type="super">12</hi> The iniquity of Ephraim <hi type="italic">is</hi> bound up; his sin <hi type="italic">is</hi> hid. <hi type="super">13</hi> The sorrows of a travailing woman shall come upon him: he <hi type="italic">is</hi> an unwise son; for he should not stay long in <hi type="italic">the place of</hi> the breaking forth of children. <hi type="super">14</hi> I will ransom them from the power of the grave; I will redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction: repentance shall be hid from mine eyes. <hi type="super">15</hi> Though he be fruitful among <hi type="italic">his</hi> brethren, an east wind shall come, the wind of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall come up from the wilderness, and his spring shall become dry, and his fountain shall be dried up: he shall spoil the treasure of all pleasant vessels. <hi type="super">16</hi> Samaria shall become desolate; for she hath rebelled against her God: they shall fall by the sword: their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up. <div eID="gen19952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19953" type="x-p"/> The first of these verses is the summary, or contents, of all the rest (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">v. 9</reference>), where we have, 1. All the blame of Israel's ruin laid upon themselves: <hi type="italic">O Israel! thy perdition is thence;</hi> it is of and from thyself; or, "<hi type="italic">It has destroyed thee, O Israel!</hi> that is, all that sin and folly of thine which thou art before charged with. As <hi type="italic">thy own wickedness</hi> has many a time <hi type="italic">corrected thee,</hi> so that has now at length destroyed thee." Note, Wilful sinners are self-destroyers. Obstinate impenitence is the grossest self-murder. Those that are <hi type="italic">destroyed of the destroyer</hi> have their blood upon their own head; they have <hi type="italic">destroyed themselves.</hi> 2. All the glory of Israel's relief ascribed to God: <hi type="italic">But in me is thy help.</hi> That is, (1.) It might have been: "I would have helped thee and healed thee, but thou wouldst not be healed and helped, but wast resolutely set upon thy own destruction." This will aggravate the condemnation of sinners, not only that they did that which tended to their own ruin, but that they opposed the offers God made them and the methods he took with them to prevent it: <hi type="italic">I would have gathered them,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">would not.</hi> They might have been easily and effectually helped, but they put the help away from them. Nay, (2.) It may be: "Thy case is bad, but it is not desperate. <hi type="italic">Thou hast destroyed thyself;</hi> but come to me, and I will help thee." This is a plank thrown out after shipwreck, and greatly magnifies not only the power of God, that he can help when things are at the worst, can help those that cannot help themselves, but the riches of his grace, that he will help those that have destroyed themselves and therefore might justly be left to perish, that he will help those that have long refused his help. Dr. Pocock gives a different reading and sense of this verse: "<hi type="italic">O Israel! this has destroyed thee, that in me is thy help.</hi> Presuming upon God and his favour has emboldened thee in those wicked ways which have been thy ruin." <div eID="gen19953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19954" type="x-p"/> Now, in the rest of these verses, we may see, <div eID="gen19954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19955" type="x-p"/> I. How Israel destroyed themselves. It is said (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.16">v. 16</reference>), They <hi type="italic">rebelled against God,</hi> revolted from their allegiance to him, entered into a confederacy with his enemies, and took up arms against him; and this was the thing that ruined them, for never any hardened themselves against God and prospered. Note, Those that rebel against their God destroy themselves, for they make him their enemy for whom they are an unequal match. <div eID="gen19955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19956" type="x-p"/> 1. They treasure up wrath against the day of wrath, and so they destroy themselves. They are doing that, every day, which will be remembered against them another day (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up, and his sin is hid;</hi> God took notice of it, kept it upon record, and will produce it against him and reckon with him for it afterwards. Their former sins contributed to their present destruction; for they were <hi type="italic">laid up in store with God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.34-Deut.32.35">Deut. xxxii. 34, 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.17">Job xiv. 17</reference>. It is laid up in safety, and will not be forgotten, nor the evidence against him lost; but it is laid up in secret; it is hid; the sinner himself is not aware of it. It is bound up in God's omniscience, in the sinner's own conscience. Note, The sin of sinners is not forgotten till it is pardoned, but an exact account is kept of it, which will be opened in proper time. <div eID="gen19956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19957" type="x-p"/> 2. They make no haste to repent and help themselves when they are under divine rebukes; they are their own ruin because they will not do what they should do towards their own salvation, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.13">v. 13</reference>. (1.) They are brought into trouble and distress by sin: <hi type="italic">The sorrows of a travailing woman shall come upon him.</hi> They shall smart for sin, and so be made sensible of it; they shall be thrown into pangs and agonies by it, very sharp and severe, and yet, like the pains of a woman in labour, hopeful and promising, and in order to deliverance; and by these, though God corrects them, yet he designs their good. They are chastened, that they may not be destroyed. But, (2.) They are not by these forwarded as they ought to be towards repentance and reformation, which would cause their sorrows to issue in true joy: <hi type="italic">He is an unwise son, for he should not stay long,</hi> as he does, <hi type="italic">in the place of the breaking forth of children,</hi> but, being <hi type="italic">brought to the birth,</hi> should struggle to <hi type="italic">get forth,</hi> lest he be stifled and <hi type="italic">still-born at last.</hi> Were the child which the mother is in travail of capable of understanding its own case, we should reckon it an unwise child that would choose to stay long in the birth; for the <hi type="italic">captive exile hasteth to be loosed, lest he die in the pit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.14">Isa. li. 14</reference>. Note, Those may justly be reckoned their own destroyers who defer and put off their repentance, by which alone they might help themselves. Those are in danger of miscarrying in conversion who delay it, and will not put forth themselves to speed the work and bring it to an issue. <div eID="gen19957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19958" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> they are destroyed because they have done that which will be their certain ruin and neglected that which would have been their only relief. Here is a sad description of the desolation they are doomed to, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.15-Hos.14.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. It is here taken for granted that <hi type="italic">Ephraim</hi> is <hi type="italic">fruitful among his children;</hi> his name signifies <hi type="italic">fruitfulness.</hi> He is fruitful in respect of the plentiful products of his country and the great numbers of its inhabitants; it was both a rich and a populous tribe, as was foretold concerning it; but sin turns this fruitful tribe into barrenness. <hi type="italic">Joseph</hi> was a <hi type="italic">fruitful bough,</hi> but for sin it was blasted. The instrument is an <hi type="italic">east wind,</hi> representing a foreign enemy that should invade it. It is called the <hi type="italic">wind of the Lord,</hi> not only because it shall be a very great and strong wind, but because it shall be sent by divine direction; it shall come <hi type="italic">from the Lord,</hi> and do whatever he appoints; and see what effect it shall have upon that flourishing tribe, what desolations war shall make. (1.) Was it a rich tribe? The foreign enemy shall make it poor enough. This <hi type="italic">wind of the Lord</hi> shall come up <hi type="italic">from the wilderness,</hi> a freezing blasting wind, and shall <hi type="italic">dry up</hi> the <hi type="italic">springs</hi> and <hi type="italic">fountains</hi> with which this tree is watered, shall exhaust the sources of its wealth. The invader shall waste the country and so impoverish the husbandman, shall intercept trade and commerce and so impoverish the merchant; and let not the great men, whose wealth lies in their rich furniture, think that they shall be exempted from the judgment, for he shall <hi type="italic">spoil the treasure of all pleasant vessels.</hi> See the folly of those that lay up their treasure on earth, that lay it up in <hi type="italic">pleasant vessels (vessels of desire,</hi> so the word is), on which they set their affections, and in which they place their comfort and satisfaction. This is treasure that may be spoiled and that they may be spoiled of; it is what either moth or rust may corrupt, or what thieves and soldiers may steal and carry away. But wise and happy are those who have laid up their treasures in heaven, and in the pleasant things of that world, which cannot be spoiled, which they cannot be stripped of; ever happy are they, and therefore truly wise. (2.) Was it a populous tribe, and numerous? The enemy shall depopulate it and make its men few: <hi type="italic">Samaria shall become desolate,</hi> without inhabitants. [1.] Those shall be cut off who are the guard and joy of the present generation; the men who bear arms shall bear them to no purpose, for <hi type="italic">they shall fall by the sword,</hi> so that there shall be none to make head against the fury of the conqueror nor to take care of the concerns either of the public or of private families. [2.] Those shall be cut off who are the seed and hope of the next generation, who should rise up in the places of those who fell by the sword; the whole nation must be rooted out, and therefore <hi type="italic">the infants shall be dashed to pieces,</hi> in the most cruel and barbarous manner, and, which is if possible yet more inhuman, <hi type="italic">the women with child shall be ripped up.</hi> Thus shall the glory of <hi type="italic">Samaria flee away from the birth, and from the womb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.9.11">ch. ix. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.14">x. 14</reference>. See instances of this cruelty, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.12">2 Kings viii. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.16">xv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.13">Amos i. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen19958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19959" type="x-p"/> II. Let us now see how God was the help of this self-destroying people, how he was their only help (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will be thy King,</hi> to rule and save thee. Though they had refused to be his subjects and had rebelled against him, yet he would still be their King and would not abandon them. The business and care of a good king is to keep his people, not only from ruined by foreign enemies, but from ruining themselves and one another. Thus will God yet be Israel's King, as he was <hi type="italic">their King of old.</hi> Note, Our case would be sad indeed if God were not better to us than we are to ourselves. <div eID="gen19959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19960" type="x-p"/> 1. God will be their King when they have no other king; he will protect and save them when those are cut off and gone who should have been their protectors and saviours: <hi type="italic">I will be he</hi> (so <reference osisRef="Hos.14.10">v. 10</reference> may be read), he that shall help thee. "<hi type="italic">Where is the king that may save thee in all thy cities,</hi> that may go in and out before thee, and fight thy battles, when thy cities are invaded by a foreign power, and suppress the more dangerous quarrels of thy citizens among themselves? <hi type="italic">Where are thy judges,</hi> who by administering public justice should preserve the public peace? For it is <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> and <hi type="italic">peace</hi> that <hi type="italic">kiss each other. Where are thy judges</hi> that thou hadst such a desire of and such a dependence upon, of whom thou saidst, <hi type="italic">Give me a king and princes?</hi> This refers, (1.) To the foolish wicked desire which the whole nation had of a kingly government, being weary of the theocracy, or divine government, which they had been under during the time of the <hi type="italic">Judges,</hi> because it looked too mean for them. They rejected Samuel, and in him <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi> when they said, <hi type="italic">Give us a king</hi> like the nations, whereas the <hi type="italic">Lord was their King.</hi> (2.) To the desire which the ten tribes had of a kingly government different from that of the house of David, because they thought that was too absolute and bore too hard upon them, and they hoped to better themselves by setting up Jeroboam. Both these are instances, [1.] Of men's improvidence for themselves. When they are uneasy with their present lot they are fond of novelty, and think to better themselves by a change; but they are commonly disappointed, and do not find that advantage in the alteration which they promised themselves. [2.] Of men's impiety towards God, in thinking to refine upon his appointments and amend them. God gave Israel judges and prophets for their guidance; but they were weary of them, and cried, <hi type="italic">Give us a king and princes.</hi> God gave them the house of David, established it by a covenant of royalty; but they were soon weary of that too, and cried, <hi type="italic">We have no part in David.</hi> Those destroy themselves who are not pleased with what God does for them, but think they can do better for themselves. Well, in both these requests, Providence humoured them, gave them Saul first, and afterwards Jeroboam. And what the better were they for them? Saul was <hi type="italic">given in anger</hi> (given in <hi type="italic">thunder,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.18-1Sam.12.19">1 Sam. xii. 18, 19</reference>) and soon after was <hi type="italic">taken away in wrath,</hi> upon Mount Gilboa. The kingly government of the ten tribes was given in anger, not only against Solomon for his defection, but against the ten tribes that desired it, for their discontent and disaffection to the house of David; and God was now about to take that away in wrath by the power of the king of Assyria. And then, <hi type="italic">where is thy King?</hi> He is gone, and thou shalt abide many days <hi type="italic">without a king, and without a prince</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">ch. iii. 4</reference>), shalt have none to save thee, none to rule thee. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God often gives in anger what we sinfully and inordinately desire, gives it with a curse, and with it gives us up to our own hearts' lusts. Thus he gave Israel quails. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What we inordinately desire we are commonly disappointed in, and it cannot save us, as we expected it should. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> What God gives in anger he takes away in wrath; what he gives because we did not desire it well he takes away because we did not use it well. It is the happiness of the saints that, whether God gives or takes, it is all in love, and furnishes them with matter for praise. <hi type="italic">To the pure all things are pure.</hi> It is the misery of the wicked that, whether God gives or takes, it is all in wrath; to them nothing is pure, nothing is comfortable. <div eID="gen19960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19961" type="x-p"/> 2. God will do that for them which no other king could do if they had one (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will ransom them from the power of the grave.</hi> Though Israel, according to the flesh, be abandoned to destruction, God has mercy in store for his spiritual Israel, in whom all the promises were to have their accomplishment, and this among the rest, for to them the apostle applies it (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.55">1 Cor. xv. 55</reference>), and particularly to the blessed resurrection of believers at the great day, yet not excluding their spiritual resurrection from the death of sin to a holy, heavenly, spiritual, and divine life. It is promised, (1.) That the captives shall be delivered, <hi type="italic">shall be ransomed, from the power of the grave.</hi> Their deliverance shall be by ransom; and we know who it was that paid their ransom, and what the ransom was, for it was the Son of man that <hi type="italic">gave his life a ransom for many,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">Matt. xx. 28</reference>. It is he that thus redeemed them. Those who, upon their repenting and believing, are, for the sake of Christ's righteousness, acquitted from the guilt of sin and saved from death and hell, which are the <hi type="italic">wages of sin,</hi> are those <hi type="italic">ransomed of the Lord</hi> that shall, in the great day, be brought out of the grave in triumph, and it shall be as impossible for the banks of death to hold them as it was to hold their Master. (2.) That the conqueror shall be destroyed: <hi type="italic">O death! I will be thy plagues.</hi> Jesus Christ was the plague and destruction of death and the grave when by death he <hi type="italic">destroyed him that had the power of death,</hi> and when in his own resurrection he triumphed over the grave. But the complete destruction of them will be in the resurrection of believers at the great day, when death shall for ever be swallowed up in victory, and it is the last enemy that shall be destroyed. But the word which we translate <hi type="italic">I will</hi> may as well be rendered <hi type="italic">Ubi nunc—Where now</hi> are thy plagues? And so the apostle took it: <hi type="italic">'O death! where is thy plague,</hi> or <hi type="italic">sting,</hi> with which thou hast so long pestered the world? <hi type="italic">O grave! where is thy victory,</hi> or thy <hi type="italic">destruction,</hi> wherewith thou has destroyed mankind?" Christ has abolished death, has broken the power of it and altered the property of it, and so enabled us to triumph over it. This promise he has made, and it shall be made good to all that are his; for <hi type="italic">repentance shall be hidden from his eyes;</hi> he will never recall this sentence passed on death and the grave, for he is not a man that he should repent. Thanks be to God therefore who gives us the victory.  <chapter eID="Hos.13"/> <div eID="gen19961" type="x-p"/>

entries.0f3062174d57b055f8f73d196a1a8de4014e5e6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12410"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.13.1-Hos.13.16">Ho 13:1-16</reference>. Ephraim's Sinful Ingratitude to God, and Its Fatal Consequence; God's Promise at Last.</title> <div sID="gen22755" type="x-p"/> This chapter and the fourteenth chapter probably belong to the troubled times that followed Pekah's murder by Hoshea (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.13.11">Ho 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.30">2Ki 15:30</reference>). The subject is the idolatry of Ephraim, notwithstanding God's past benefits, destined to be his ruin.<div eID="gen22755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12410"/><hi type="bold">1. When Ephraim spake trembling--</hi>rather, "When Ephraim (the tribe most powerful among the twelve in Israel's early history) spake (authoritatively) there was trembling"; all reverentially feared him [Jerome], (compare <reference osisRef="Job.29.8">Job 29:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.9.21">9, 21</reference>).<div eID="gen22756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">offended in Baal--</hi>that is, in respect to Baal, by worshipping him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.31">1Ki 16:31</reference>), under Ahab; a more heinous offense than even the calves. Therefore it is at this climax of guilt that Ephraim "died." Sin has, in the sight of God, within itself the germ of death, though that death may not visibly take effect till long after. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.7.9">Ro 7:9</reference>, "Sin revived, and I died." So Adam in the day of his sin was to die, though the sentence was not visibly executed till long after (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.17">Ge 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.5">5:5</reference>). Israel is similarly represented as politically dead in <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.1-Ezek.37.28">Eze 37:1-28</reference>. <div eID="gen22757" type="x-p"/>
entries.a472e2c2d4e7238e419c38d7e95a19d4d96853b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12411"/><div sID="gen22758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12411"/><hi type="bold">2. according to their own understanding--</hi>that is, their arbitrary devising. Compare "will-worship," <reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>. Men are not to be "wise above that which is written," or to follow their own understanding, but God's command in worship.<div eID="gen22758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kiss the calves--</hi>an act of adoration to the golden calves (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.18">1Ki 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.27">Job 31:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Psa 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen22759" type="x-p"/>
entries.1adea5ddd1d6360a7e9be61edc3a419c999e8147: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12412"/><div sID="gen22760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12412"/><hi type="bold">3. they shall be as the morning cloud ... dew--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">Ho 6:4</reference>). As their "goodness" soon vanished like the morning cloud and dew, so they shall perish like them.<div eID="gen22760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the floor--</hi>the threshing-floor, generally an open area, on a height, exposed to the winds.<div eID="gen22761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chimney--</hi>generally in the East an orifice in the wall, at once admitting the light, and giving egress to the smoke. <div eID="gen22762" type="x-p"/>

(<reference osisRef="Hos.12.9">Ho 12:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.11">Is 43:11</reference>).<div eID="gen22763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no saviour--</hi>temporal as well as spiritual.<div eID="gen22764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">besides me--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">Is 45:21</reference>). <div eID="gen22765" type="x-p"/>
entries.18f82fcfd5fef6589b04db26e70d497963cfbb6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12414"/><div sID="gen22766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12414"/><hi type="bold">5. I did know thee--</hi>did acknowledge thee as Mine, and so took care of thee (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.3">Psa 144:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Am 3:2</reference>). As I knew thee as Mine, so thou shouldest know no God but Me (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.4">Ho 13:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... land of ... drought--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">De 8:15</reference>). <div eID="gen22767" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9fa5a1e5be5aaaff0f0f4b0cdba4126d8620e10: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12415"/><div sID="gen22768" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12415"/>6. Image from cattle, waxing wanton in abundant pasture (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.2.5">Ho 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.13-Deut.32.15">De 32:13-15</reference>). In proportion as I fed them to the full, they were so satiated that "their heart was exalted"; a sad contrast to the time when, by God's blessing, Ephraim truly "exalted himself in Israel" (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.1">Ho 13:1</reference>).<div eID="gen22768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore have they forgotten me--</hi>the very reason why men should remember God (namely, prosperity, which comes from Him) is the cause often of their forgetting Him. God had warned them of this danger (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.11">De 6:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen22769" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f7019ef8fe444dbcfe8f135db7af7753db0351a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12416"/><div sID="gen22770" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12416"/>7. (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Ho 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.10">La 3:10</reference>).<div eID="gen22770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leopard--</hi>The Hebrew comes from a root meaning "spotted" (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.13.23">Jr 13:23</reference>). Leopards lurk in thickets and thence spring on their victims.<div eID="gen22771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">observe--</hi>that is, lie in wait for them. Several manuscripts, the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic read, by a slight change of the Hebrew vowel pointing, "by the way of Assyria," a region abounding in leopards and lions. English Version is better. <div eID="gen22772" type="x-p"/>
entries.8543863234bcbe6725b51b6e773b4bf0fdb60039: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12417"/><div sID="gen22773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12417"/>8. "Writers on the natures of beasts say that none is more savage than a she bear, when bereaved of her whelps" [Jerome].<div eID="gen22773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">caul of ... heart--</hi>the membrane enclosing it: the pericardium.<div eID="gen22774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there--</hi>"by the way" (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.7">Ho 13:7</reference>). <div eID="gen22775" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8618d85ee15101252648cc21c70af936336d586: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12418"/><div sID="gen22776" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12418"/><hi type="bold">9. thou ... in me--</hi>in contrast.<div eID="gen22776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hast destroyed thyself--</hi>that is, thy destruction is of thyself (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.32">Pr 6:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">8:36</reference>).<div eID="gen22777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in me is thine help--</hi>literally, "in thine help" (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.33.26">De 33:26</reference>). Hadst thou rested thy hope in Me, I would have been always ready at hand for thy help [Grotius]. <div eID="gen22778" type="x-p"/>
entries.9be723fb5c5c8b5a466617651e21c3ff899dd5d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12419"/><div sID="gen22779" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12419"/><hi type="bold">10. I will be thy king; where--</hi>rather, as the Margin and the Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, "Where now is thy king?" [Maurer]. English Version is, however, favored both by the Hebrew, by the antithesis between Israel's self-chosen and perishing kings, and God, Israel's abiding King (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen22779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">where ... Give me a king--</hi>Where now is the king whom ye substituted in My stead? Neither Saul, whom the whole nation begged for, not contented with Me their true king (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.5">1Sa 8:5</reference>, 7, 19, 20; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.19">10:19</reference>), nor Jeroboam, whom subsequently the ten tribes chose instead of the line of David My anointed, can save thee now. They had expected from their kings what is the prerogative of God alone, namely, the power of saving them.<div eID="gen22780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judges--</hi>including all civil authorities under the king (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.2.3">Am 2:3</reference>). <div eID="gen22781" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f0dc6d376beec534b449060320977c6cac74a85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12420"/><div sID="gen22782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12420"/><hi type="bold">11. I gave ... king in ... anger ... took ... away in ... wrath--</hi>true both of Saul (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.22">1Sa 15:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.1">16:1</reference>) and of Jeroboam's line (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.30">2Ki 15:30</reference>). Pekah was taken away through Hoshea, as he himself took away Pekahiah; and as Hoshea was soon to be taken away by the Assyrian king. <div eID="gen22782" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4995e285b7918fae334fdb51137b9a232bf6d47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12421"/><div sID="gen22783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12421"/><hi type="bold">12. bound up ... hid--</hi>Treasures, meant to be kept, are bound up and hidden; that is, do not flatter yourselves, because of the delay, that I have forgotten your sin. Nay (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.9">Ho 9:9</reference>), Ephraim's iniquity is kept as it were safely sealed up, until the due time comes for bringing it forth for punishment (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.34">De 32:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.17">Job 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.19">21:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.2.5">Ro 2:5</reference>). Opposed to "blotting out the handwriting against" the sinner (<reference osisRef="Col.2.14">Col 2:14</reference>). <div eID="gen22783" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6220e4c31aa7b5582dd2f7a7f29e7e3b9639d38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12422"/><div sID="gen22784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12422"/><hi type="bold">13. sorrows of a travailing woman--</hi>calamities sudden and agonizing (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.6">Jr 30:6</reference>).<div eID="gen22784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unwise--</hi>in not foreseeing the impending judgment, and averting it by penitence (<reference osisRef="Prov.22.3">Pr 22:3</reference>).<div eID="gen22785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he should not stay long in the place of the breaking forth of children--</hi>When Israel might deliver himself from calamity by the pangs of penitence, he brings ruin on himself by so long deferring a new birth unto repentance, like a child whose mother has not strength to bring it forth, and which therefore remains so long in the passage from the womb as to run the risk of death (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.3">2Ki 19:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.3">Is 37:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.9">66:9</reference>). <div eID="gen22786" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c50ffc8a159b029e1d6aa322bdf9f13b3af88ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12423"/><div sID="gen22787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12423"/>14. Applying primarily to God's restoration of Israel from Assyria partially, and, in times yet future, fully from all the lands of their present long-continued dispersion, and political death (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.6.2">Ho 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">Is 25:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">26:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.12">Eze 37:12</reference>). God's power and grace are magnified in quickening what to the eye of flesh seems dead and hopeless (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.17">Ro 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.19">19</reference>). As Israel's history, past and future, has a representative character in relation to the Church, this verse is expressed in language alluding to Messiah's (who is the ideal Israel) grand victory over the grave and death, the first-fruits of His own resurrection, the full harvest to come at the general resurrection; hence the similarity between this verse and Paul's language as to the latter (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.55">1Co 15:55</reference>). That similarity becomes more obvious by translating as the Septuagint, from which Paul plainly quotes; and as the same Hebrew word is translated in <reference osisRef="Hos.13.10">Ho 13:10</reference>, "O death, where are thy plagues (paraphrased by the Septuagint, 'thy victory')? O grave, where is thy destruction (rendered by the Septuagint, 'thy sting')?" The question is that of one triumphing over a foe, once a cruel tyrant, but now robbed of all power to hurt.<div eID="gen22787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">repentance shall be hid from mine eyes--</hi>that is, I will not change My purpose of fulfilling My promise by delivering Israel, on the condition of their return to Me (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.14.2-Hos.14.8">Ho 14:2-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.23.19">Nu 23:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.29">Ro 11:29</reference>). <div eID="gen22788" type="x-p"/>
entries.943a54ea470908888e35a903f1f9c259cf818359: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12424"/><div sID="gen22789" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12424"/><hi type="bold">15. fruitful--</hi>referring to the meaning of "Ephraim," from a Hebrew root, "to be fruitful" (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.52">Ge 41:52</reference>). It was long the most numerous and flourishing of the tribes (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.19">Ge 48:19</reference>).<div eID="gen22789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wind of the Lord--</hi>that is, sent by the Lord (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.40.7">Is 40:7</reference>), who has His instruments of punishment always ready. The Assyrian, Shalmaneser, &c., is meant (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.11">Jr 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.17">18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.12">Eze 19:12</reference>).<div eID="gen22790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the wilderness--</hi>that is, the desert part of Syria (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.15">1Ki 19:15</reference>), the route from Assyria into Israel.<div eID="gen22791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>the Assyrian invader. Shalmaneser began the siege of Samaria in 723 <hi type="bold">B.C. Its close was in 721 B.C., the first year of Sargon, who seems to have usurped the throne of Assyria while Shalmaneser was at the siege of Samaria. Hence, while <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:6</reference> states, "the king of Assyria took Samaria," <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.10">2Ki 18:10</reference> says, "at the end of three years they took it." In Sargon's magnificent palace at Khorsabad, inscriptions mention the number--</hi>27,280--of Israelites carried captive from Samaria and other places of Israel by the founder of the palace [G. V. Smith]. <div eID="gen22792" type="x-p"/>
entries.70678c9795ec4a52a4dff031da3becd305dafee1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12425"/><div sID="gen22793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12425"/>16. This verse and <reference osisRef="Hos.13.15">Ho 13:15</reference> foretell the calamities about to befall Israel before her restoration (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.14">Ho 13:14</reference>), owing to her impenitence.<div eID="gen22793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her God--</hi>the greatest aggravation of her rebellion, that it was against her God (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.4">Ho 13:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">infants ... dashed in pieces, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.12">2Ki 8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.16">15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.1.13">Am 1:13</reference>). <chapter eID="Hos.13"/>

entries.b570bc34049067e452f88630cd246d4d928b8e10: <div eID="gen33920" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33921" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33922" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33922" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33921" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33923" type="x-p"/> Thus chapter begins with observing that the fear of God leads to prosperity, but sin to ruin; a truth most visibly exemplified in the sin and punishment of Ephraim, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.1-Hos.13.3">Hos 13:1-3</reference>. As an aggravation of their guilt, God reminds them of his former favors, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.4">Hos 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.5">Hos 13:5</reference>; which they had shamefully abused, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.6">Hos 13:6</reference>; and which now expose them to dreadful punishments, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.7">Hos 13:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.8">Hos 13:8</reference>. He, however, tempers these awful threatenings with gracious promises; and, on their repentance, engages to save them, when no other could protect them, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.9-Hos.13.11">Hos 13:9-11</reference>. But, alas! instead of repenting, Ephraim is filling up the measure of his iniquity, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.12">Hos 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.13">Hos 13:13</reference>. Notwithstanding this, God promises to put forth has almighty power in behalf of his people, and, as it were, raise them from the dead, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.14">Hos 13:14</reference>; although, in the meantime, they must be visited with great national calamities, compared first to the noxious and parching east wind, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.15">Hos 13:15</reference>, and described immediately after in the plainest terms, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.16">Hos 13:16</reference>. <div eID="gen33923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33924" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33925" type="x-p"/> When Ephraim spake trembling - When he was meek and humble, of a broken heart and contrite spirit. <div eID="gen33925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33926" type="x-p"/> He exalted himself in Israel - He became great in God's sight; he rose in the Divine esteem in proportion as he sank in his own. But this did not continue. <div eID="gen33926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33927" type="x-p"/> He offended in Baal - He became an idolater. <div eID="gen33927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33928" type="x-p"/> He died - The sentence of death from the Divine justice went out against him. <div eID="gen33928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33929" type="x-p"/> This has been differently understood: "As soon as Ephraim spake (To your tents, O Israel!) There was a trembling or commotion: then the kingdom was exalted in Israel." Thus taken, it refers to the division of the ten tribes from Rehoboam, son of Solomon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.16">1Kgs 12:16</reference>, etc., and the establishment of the kingdom of Israel under Jeroboam in opposition to that of Judah; which breach was never healed.
entries.d98ac8bb3b278b9b74a84b7eb217c3a2d9acf667: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33930" type="x-p"/> And now they sin more and more - They increase in every kind of vice, having abandoned the great Inspirer of virtue. <div eID="gen33930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33931" type="x-p"/> Let the men that sacrifice kiss the calves - This was the test. If there be a Jew that pretends to sacrifice, and whose conversion is dubious, let him come openly and kiss the calves. This will show what he is; no real Jew will do this. If he be an idolater, he will not scruple. This was the ancient method of adoration. <div eID="gen33931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33932" type="x-p"/> 1. They kissed the idol. <div eID="gen33932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33933" type="x-p"/> 2. When the statue was too high or too far off, they presented the hand, in token of alliance. <div eID="gen33933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33934" type="x-p"/> 3. They brought that hand respectfully to their mouths, and kissed it. <div eID="gen33934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33935" type="x-p"/> This was the genuine act of adoration; from ad, to, and os, oris, the mouth. So Pliny, Hist. Nat., lib. xxviii., c. 1. Adorando, dexteram ad oscula referimus. <div eID="gen33935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33936" type="x-p"/> And Apuleius, Asin., lib. iv: <div eID="gen33936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33937" type="x-p"/> Admoventes oribus suis dexteram, ut ipsam prorsus deam religiosis adorationibus venerabantur. <div eID="gen33937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33938" type="x-p"/> See Calmet, and see the note on <reference osisRef="Job.31.17">Job 31:17</reference>.
entries.ec571aca4c40f8813cd2d726f593d65540dc9839: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33939" type="x-p"/> Therefore they shall be as the morning Cloud - as the early Dew - as the Chaff - as the Smoke - Four things, most easy to be driven about and dissipated, are employed here to show how they should be scattered among the nations, and dissipated by captivity.
entries.f47f3142a660eacd9801bb2320ec5de139601686: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33940" type="x-p"/> I am the Lord thy God - This was the first discovery I made of myself to you, and the first commandment I gave; and I showed you that besides me there was no Savior. There is a remarkable addition in the Septuagint here: "But I am Jehovah thy God, who stretched out the heavens and created the earth. And I showed them not to thee, that thou shouldest walk after them. And I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt," etc. This might have been once in the Hebrew text.
entries.55be827d6e00e4ef302e31830d46b1c3e587a58f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33941" type="x-p"/> I did know thee - I approved of thee; I loved thee; and by miraculously providing for thee in that land of drought, I demonstrated my love.
entries.54418959eda41f01bfee7fdd9d72283e0d99cafc: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33942" type="x-p"/> According to their pasture - They had a rich pasture, and were amply supplied with every good. They became exalted in their heart, forgat their God, and became a prey to their enemies. "He that exalteth himself shall be abased."
entries.4da29f628e46d3fba87efe5011524985fb2a5e80: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33943" type="x-p"/> I will be unto them as a lion - שחל shachal is supposed to mean here the black lion, frequent in Ethiopia. <div eID="gen33943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33944" type="x-p"/> As a leopard - נמר namar, so termed from its spotted skin, for to be spotted is the signification of the root. <div eID="gen33944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33945" type="x-p"/> Will I observe them - The leopard, tiger, and panther will hide themselves in thick bushwood, near where they expect any prey to pass; and as soon as it comes near, spring suddenly upon it. To this is the allusion in the text: "By the way will I observe them;" watch for them as the leopard does. They shall be greatly harassed even on their way to Assyria, when going into captivity.
entries.163f64dac66784286238e877dca7f80318c8a912: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33946" type="x-p"/> As a bear - bereaved - This is a figure to denote excessive ferocity. See the note on <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.8">2Sam 17:8</reference> (note), where a remarkable instance is given. <div eID="gen33946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33947" type="x-p"/> And will rend the caul of their heart - Every savage beast goes first to the seat of the blood when it has seized its prey; as in this fluid they delight more than in the most delicate parts of the flesh. <div eID="gen33947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33948" type="x-p"/> There will I devour them like a lion - לביא labi, the old strong lion; drinking the blood, tearing the flesh, and breaking the bones to extract the marrow. <div eID="gen33948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33949" type="x-p"/> The wild beast shall tear them - Probably this refers to the chakal or jackal, who frequently hunts down the prey, which the lion takes the liberty to devour, while the jackal stands by, and afterwards picks the bones. Hence he has been called the lion's Provider, and the lion's waiting-man.
entries.f18b654100f4b3a44dff6940ef0d87d5917e732e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33950" type="x-p"/> O Israel, thou hast destroyed thyself - These evils come not by my immediate infliction; they are the consequences of thy own crimes. In the above terrifying figures of the ferocious beasts, the prophet only shows what they would meet with from the hand of the Assyrians in the war, the famine, and the captivity; God being represented as doing what he only permits to be done. <div eID="gen33950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33951" type="x-p"/> But in me is thine help - "Though thou hast destroyed thyself, yet in me alone can thy help be found" - Newcome. And others read, And who will help thee? reading מי mi, who, for בי bi, in me. Though this is countenanced by the Syriac, yet there is no evidence of it in any of the MSS. yet collated, nor do I think it to be the true reading.
entries.9d6ad58eed836639d91f7318c387eaeee0f740a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33952" type="x-p"/> Give me a king and princes? - Referring to the time in which they cast off the Divine theocracy and chose Saul in the place of Jehovah.
entries.b236baaddd1161d6484805df60aafb326c41501a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33953" type="x-p"/> I gave thee a king in mine anger - Such was Saul; for they highly offended God when they clamoured to have a king like the heathen nations that were around them. <div eID="gen33953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33954" type="x-p"/> Took him away in my wrath - Permitted him and the Israelites to fall before the Philistines. Others think that Shalmaneser was the king thus given, and Hoshea the king thus taken away.
entries.fee47ac6de43df321a9fdafb980223a10f09eed5: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33955" type="x-p"/> The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up - It is registered in my court of justice; the death warrant is in store, and will be produced in due time. Though there be not at present the judgment inflicted which such glaring transgressions demand, yet it will surely come. Such crimes cannot go unpunished.
entries.a22b38447ff208e5063e5c8889068ad6ff4f8a77: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33956" type="x-p"/> The sorrows of a travailing woman - These judgments shall come suddenly and unavoidably. <div eID="gen33956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33957" type="x-p"/> The place of the breaking forth of children - As there is a critical time in parturition in which the mother in hard labor may by skillful assistants be eased of her burden, which, if neglected, may endanger the life both of parent and child, so there was a time in which Ephraim might have returned to God, but they would not; therefore they are now in danger of being finally destroyed. And, speaking after the manner of men, he must be deemed an unwise son, who if he had power and consideration, would prolong his stay in the porch of life, where he must necessarily be suffocated; so is Ephraim, who, though warned of his danger, having yet power to escape, continued in his sin, and is now come to destruction. I could illustrate the allusion in the text farther, and show the accurate propriety of the original; but the subject forbids it.
entries.3af540c61dd27f0aa7907922ecc1b82c71756dad: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33958" type="x-p"/> I will ransom them from the power of the grave - In their captivity they are represented as dead and buried, which is a similar view to that taken of the Jews in the Babylonish captivity by Ezekiel in his vision of the valley of dry bones. They are now lost as to the purpose for which they were made, for which God had wrought so many miracles for them and for their ancestors; but the gracious purpose of God shall not be utterly defeated. He will bring them out of that grave, and ransom them from that death; for as they have deserved that death and disgraceful burial, they must be redeemed and ransomed from it, or still lie under it. And who can do this but God himself? And he will do it. In the prospect of this the prophet exclaims, in the person of the universal Redeemer, "O death, I will be thy plagues;" I will bring into thy reign the principle of its destruction. The Prince of life shall lie for a time under thy power, that he may destroy that power. <div eID="gen33958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33959" type="x-p"/> O grave, I will be thy destruction - I will put an end to thy dreary domination by rising from the dead, and bringing life and immortality to life by my Gospel, and by finally raising from the death the whole human race in the day of the general resurrection. שאול sheol, which we translate grave, is the state of the dead. מות maveth, which we translate death, is the principle of corruption that renders the body unfit to be longer the tenement of the soul, and finally decomposes it. Sheol shall be destroyed, for it must deliver up all its dead. Maveth shall be annihilated, for the body shall be raised incorruptible. See the use which the apostle makes of this passage, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.54">1Cor 15:54</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.55">1Cor 15:55</reference>; but he does not quote from the Hebrew, nor from any of the ancient versions. He had to apply the subject anew; and the Spirit, which had originally given the words, chose to adapt them to the subject then in hand, which was the resurrection of the dead in the last day. Instead of דבריך debareycha, thy plagues, one of my oldest MSS., ninety-six of Kennicott's and thirty-two of De Rossi's, have דברך debarcha, thy plague, that which shall carry thee off, as the plague does them who are affected by it. To carry off, carry away, is one of the regular meanings of the verb דבר dabar. <div eID="gen33959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33960" type="x-p"/> Repentance shall be hid from mine eyes - On these points I will not change my purpose; this is the signification of repentance when attributed to God.
entries.9dd51c3c54b420433152e7f03c0ae0f0d9544a6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen33960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33961" type="x-p"/> Though he be fruitful - יפריא yaphri; a paronomasia on the word אפרים ephrayim, which comes from the same root פרה parah, to be fruitful, to sprout, to bud. <div eID="gen33961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33962" type="x-p"/> An east wind shall come - As the east wind parches and blasts all vegetation, so shall Shalmaneser blast and destroy the Israelitish state.
entries.715bb0feca1fb46bce24ab2049674d9167e8e5d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen33962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33963" type="x-p"/> Samaria shall become desolate - This was the capital of the Israelitish kingdom. What follows is a simple prophetic declaration of the cruelties which should be exercised upon this hapless people by the Assyrians in the sackage of the city.  <chapter eID="Hos.13"/> <div eID="gen33963" type="x-p"/>

entries.187fbb1b211e0ca341da399d5dddcfa25c54fdc7: Hos 13:1-2 <div eID="gen16267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16268" type="x-p"/> Because Israel would not desist from its idolatry, and entirely forgot the goodness of its God, He would destroy its might and glory (Hos 13:1-8). Because it did not acknowledge the Lord as its help, its throne would be annihilated along with its capital; but this judgment would become to all that were penitent a regeneration to newness of life. Hos 13:1. <hi type="italic">“When Ephraim spake, there was terror; he exalted himself in Israel; then he offended through Baal, and died.</hi> Hos 13:2. <hi type="italic">And now they continue to sin, and make themselves molten images out of their silver, idols according to their understanding: manufacture of artists is it all: they say of them, Sacrificers of men: let them kiss calves.” </hi> In order to show how deeply Israel had fallen through its apostasy, the prophet points to the great distinction which the tribe of Ephraim formerly enjoyed among the tribes of Israel. The two clauses of <hi type="italic">Hos 13:1</hi> cannot be so connected together as that נשׂא should be taken as a continuation of the infinitive דּבּר. The emphatic הוּא is irreconcilable with this. We must rather take רתת (ἁπ. λεγ., in Aramaean = רטט, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.24">Jer 49:24</reference>, terror, <hi type="italic">tremor</hi>) as the apodosis to <hi type="italic">kedabbēr</hi> 'Ephraim (when Ephraim spake), like שׂאת in <reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen 4:7</reference> : “As Ephraim spake there was terror,” i.e., men listened with fear and trembling (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.29.21">Job 29:21</reference>). נשׂא is used intransitively, as in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.5">Nah 1:5</reference>; Psa 89:10. Ephraim, i.e., the tribe of Ephraim, “exalted itself in Israel,” - not “it was distinguished among its brethren” (Hitzig), but “it raised itself to the government.” The prophet has in his mind the attempts made by Ephraim to get the rule among the tribes, which led eventually to the secession of the ten tribes from the royal family of David, and the establishment of the kingdom of Israel by the side of that of Judah. When Ephraim had secured this, the object of its earnest endeavours, it offended through Baal; i.e., not only through the introduction of the worship of Baal in the time of Ahab (1Ki 16:31.), but even through the establishment of the worship of the calves under Jeroboam (1Ki 12:28), through which Jehovah was turned into a Baal. ויּמת, used of the state or kingdom, is equivalent to “was given up to destruction” (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">Amo 2:2</reference>). The dying commenced with the introduction of the unlawful worship (cf. 1Ki 12:30). From this sin Ephraim (the people of the ten tribes) did not desist: they still continue to sin, and make themselves molten images, etc., contrary to the express prohibition in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.4">Lev 19:4</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.20.4">Exo 20:4</reference>). These words are not merely to be understood as signifying, that they added other idolatrous images in Gilgal and Beersheba to the golden calves (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">Amo 8:14</reference>); but they also involve their obstinate adherence to the idolatrous worship introduced by Jeroboam (compare 2Ki 17:16). בּתבוּדם from תּבוּנה, with the feminine termination dropped on account of the suffix (according to Ewald, §257, <hi type="italic">d</hi>; although in the note Ewald regards this formation as questionable, and doubts the correctness of the reading): “according to their understanding,” i.e., their proficiency in art. <div eID="gen16268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16269" type="x-p"/> The meaning of the second hemistich, which is very difficult, depends chiefly upon the view we take of זבחי אדם, viz., whether we render these words “they who sacrifice men,” as the lxx, the fathers, and many of the rabbins and Christian expositors have done; or “the sacrificers of (among) men,” as Kimchi, Bochart, Ewald, and others do, after the analogy of אביוני אדם in Isa 29:19. Apart from this, however, <hi type="italic">zōbhechē 'âdâm</hi> cannot possibly be taken as an independent sentence, such as “they sacrifice men,” or “human sacrificers are they,” unless with the lxx we change the participle זבחי arbitrarily into the perfect זבחוּ. As the words read, they must be connected with what follows or with what precedes. But if we connect them with what follows, we fail to obtain any suitable thought, whether we render it “human sacrificers (those who sacrifice men) kiss calves,” or “the sacrificers among men kiss calves.” The former is open to the objection that human sacrifices were not offered to the calves (i.e., to Jehovah, as worshipped under the symbol of a calf), but only to Moloch, and that the worshippers of Moloch did not kiss calves. The latter, “men who offer sacrifice kiss calves,” might indeed be understood in this sense, that the prophet intended thereby to denounce the great folly, that men should worship animals; but this does not suit the preceding words הם אמרים, and it is impossible to see in what sense they could be employed. There is no other course left, therefore, than to connect <hi type="italic">Zōbhechē 'âdâm</hi> with what precedes, though not in the way proposed by Ewald, viz., “even to these do sacrificers of men say.” This rendering is open to the following objections: (1) that הם after להם would have to be taken as an emphatic repetition of the pronoun, and we cannot find any satisfactory ground for this; and, (2) what is still more important, the fact that <hi type="italic">'âmâr</hi> would be used absolutely, in the sense of “they speak in prayer,” which, even apart from the “prayer,” cannot be sustained by any other analogous example. These difficulties vanish if we take <hi type="italic">Zōbhechē 'âdâm</hi> as an explanatory apposition to <hi type="italic">hēm</hi>: “of them (the <hi type="italic">‛ătsabbı̄m</hi>) they say, viz., the sacrificers from among men (i.e., men who sacrifice), Let them worship calves.” By the apposition <hi type="italic">zōbhechē 'âdâm</hi>, and the fact that the object <hi type="italic">‛ăgâlı̄m</hi> is placed first, so that it stands in immediate contrast to <hi type="italic">'âdâm</hi>, the absurdity of men kissing calves, i.e., worshipping them with kisses (see at 1Ki 19:18), is painted as it were before the eye.
